title: How To Send Students To Time-Out
author: Michael Linsin
summary: This article details a ten-step protocol for using time-out effectively as a classroom management consequence. Key elements include having a dedicated, separated time-out desk, sending students immediately and without lecturing when a rule triggers the consequence, requiring students to still complete class work while excluded from participation and interaction, and moving on quickly rather than turning the send-off into an interruption. Linsin describes a graduated return process - checking in after about fifteen minutes if the student is behaving well, requiring the student to raise a hand and demonstrate contrition before returning, and then welcoming them back warmly without holding a grudge. He closes by noting that, like any classroom management procedure, time-out must be explicitly taught through modeling, role-play, and practice before it can be used effectively.
points: Time-out requires a dedicated, physically separated desk and should only be triggered by rules stated in the classroom management plan.
Consequences should be delivered quickly and without a lecture, scolding, or added commentary.
Students in time-out remain accountable for classwork but are excluded from participating with the class.
Return from time-out is graduated: a check-in after about fifteen minutes, then a hand-raise and demonstrated contrition before rejoining.
Time-out, like any procedure, must be explicitly taught through modeling, role-play, and practice before implementation.
quotes: Time-out should take place at a desk separated from classmates. It’s best to have one or two strictly for this purpose.
Only send students to time-out if their behavior triggers such a consequence (as is stated in your classroom management plan). Time-out should never be a choice you make.
But be quick and direct. And never add a lecture, a scolding, or your two cents worth. Let time-out be the only consequence.
Don’t escort students to time-out. Simply inform them and then move on with whatever you were doing. Time-out should never be an interruption.
Students placed in time-out are no longer part of the class, and they need to feel excluded. Not as a punishment per se, but as a message that anyone who interferes with learning is not welcome.
When a student in time-out decides they’re ready to follow rules and be part of the class again, they must raise their hand and wait for you.
When a student is ready to return from time-out, welcome them back. A simple “Good to have you back” will do. Never hold a grudge, give a cold shoulder, or be short with them.
